title: The Pietists
hook: Spener and the Pietists gather small groups to read the Bible and live it warmly

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal's night of fire, one word sewn into a coat. Your line was fire.

What happens to a sermon after the last hymn? People shake hands at the door, go home, eat lunch. By Tuesday, it's mostly gone. A Lutheran pastor in Frankfurt named Philipp Jakob Spener worried about exactly that. His church had careful teaching, strong doctrine, faithful services. And yet faith, to him, seemed to stop at the church door. So he tried something small. He invited a few people to his house during the week to talk over the sermon and read the Bible together. Not a new church. Just a few chairs, an open book, and a question: how do we actually live this?

Spener wrote his hopes for the church in a short book called Pia Desideria, a Latin title usually rendered as pious longings, or heartfelt desires. Among them: that ordinary Christians would read the whole Bible, not just hear bits of it on Sunday. That every believer would take part in the church's life, not only the clergy, an echo of Luther's priesthood of all believers. That faith would show up in love, in how people actually treated each other. And that arguments about doctrine would be carried on with charity, not cruelty. The small groups that met in his home and others like them were sometimes called gatherings of piety. Critics called them Pietists, and in time the movement carried the name. Spener wasn't trying to throw out Lutheran teaching. He was trying to warm it. The Pietists spoke of a heart religion: faith you don't just agree to, but live. They found a model in the letter of James, in the King James words: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only." And Jesus' promise in Matthew sets the size: "where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." The movement had its tensions; some church leaders worried small groups would split congregations, and the Pietists argued about that among themselves. But the idea traveled. A Bible study or house group today can look a lot like Spener's living room.

Bring to mind two or three people you could sit with, at a kitchen table or on a video call, to read something that matters and talk about living it. Hold their faces in the quiet. If you pray, pray for them by name or rest with where two or three are gathered; if you don't, simply hold the picture of that table.
The Pietists. A movement inside Lutheran churches, sparked by Spener, that gathered small groups to read the Bible together and live their faith warmly.
Your line: a heart religion. Faith that walks out the church door with you. See you tomorrow.
